title: I Made a Big Mistake: Keep the Pawn in Reserve
summary: Coordinate king and knight, use d3 with check, then hold the pawn back to trap an underpromoted knight.

nodes.question: How can White stop g-promotion without letting the king capture d2?
nodes.explanation: White Ke6/Nb7/d2 faces Black Kc6/g4. Stopping the g-pawn is not enough: the knight must also keep the black king away from d2.

nodes.question: Should White take the g2 pawn immediately?
nodes.explanation: The knight controls g2 and d3. Moving it to g2 releases d3 to Black’s king.

nodes.question: Which piece should move after Black’s knight underpromotion?
nodes.explanation: The black knight on g1 has few safe squares. White can use a king move to complete the cage while preserving d3-d4 as a reserve tempo.

branches.title: Coordinate first, then preserve the pawn tempo
commentary: White Ke6/Nb7/d2 faces Black Kc6/g4. Stopping the g-pawn is not enough: the knight must also keep the black king away from d2.
Nd8+ checks the king while choosing a route through e6 and f4. The direct Nd6 blockade gives up the win.
Kc5 stays near the d-pawn’s path. Black aims to overload the knight with two tasks.
Ke5 takes the opposition and vacates e6 for the knight. White coordinates the king and knight instead of merely chasing the pawn.
g3 makes the promotion threat urgent. White must control g2 without surrendering the d-pawn.
Ne6+ checks c5 and steers the knight toward f4. This forcing route gains time.
Kc4 brings the king toward d3, threatening to blockade or collect White’s pawn.
Nf4 controls both g2 and d3. This necessary intermediate knight move is visible in the saved board sequence.
g2 attacks neither knight nor king, but threatens promotion and tempts a premature capture.
d3+ uses the pawn before capturing on g2. The pawn check forces the black king to choose a less convenient square.
Kc3 keeps contact with the d-pawn and makes a future knight underpromotion a drawing resource if White rushes.
Ke4 keeps d3 defended and controls f3, helping to cage a black knight born on g1.
g1=N avoids the knight fork that a queen promotion would allow. Black hopes to trade this knight for White’s final pawn.
Ke3 is the precise waiting move. The king controls f2 and f3, and Nf4 controls e2 and h3, so every escape of Ng1 loses the knight. White keeps the d-pawn in reserve.
Kb2 steps away from the pawn. This is the source’s illustrated lower king route.
d4 now advances with the white king positioned to restrict the trapped knight.
Kc3 approaches the pawn again but cannot recover the earlier drawing blockade in time.
d5 keeps the exact White win. The line stops here rather than assuming a particular further black king or knight reply.
branches.explanation: d5 keeps the exact White win. The line stops here rather than assuming a particular further black king or knight reply.

branches.title: Direct blockade only draws
commentary: White Ke6/Nb7/d2 faces Black Kc6/g4. Stopping the g-pawn is not enough: the knight must also keep the black king away from d2.
Nd6 gives up the exact win. The knight can approach the g-pawn, but the black king gains access to the d-pawn.
g3 keeps the knight occupied with promotion.
Nc4 follows the illustrated route toward the kingside.
g2 forces White to continue stopping promotion.
Ne5 prepares Nf3 and controls key central squares for now.
Kc5 advances toward the d-pawn while White spends knight tempi.
Nf3 blockades g1 but no longer denies the black king access to c4.
Kc4 gets close enough to overload the knight.
d4 tries to save the pawn by advancing it.
g1=Q offers the promoted queen to pull the knight away from d4.
Nxg1 removes the queen, but Black has achieved the diversion.
Kxd4 removes White’s last pawn. King and knight versus king is drawn.
branches.explanation: Kxd4 removes White’s last pawn. King and knight versus king is drawn.

branches.title: Capturing g2 releases the king
commentary: Begin after the forcing route has put Nf4 against Kc4/g2.
Nxg2 removes the passer but releases d3. White throws away the win by abandoning the knight’s second task.
Kd3 blockades the remaining pawn. The exact ending is drawn; winning the g-pawn alone did not solve White’s problem.
branches.explanation: Kd3 blockades the remaining pawn. The exact ending is drawn; winning the g-pawn alone did not solve White’s problem.

branches.title: Advance the pawn before improving the king
commentary: Begin after d3+ Kc3 Ke4 g1=N, with White to move.
d4 spends the reserve pawn tempo too early. The exact knight ending is drawn with best play; White needed Ke3 to finish the cage first.
branches.explanation: d4 spends the reserve pawn tempo too early. The exact knight ending is drawn with best play; White needed Ke3 to finish the cage first.

branches.title: The king retreats and the knight falls
commentary: Compare the illustrated upper king retreat after the same knight underpromotion.
Ke3 traps Ng1 while retaining the pawn on d3.
Kb4 moves away from the trapped knight. This is the source’s alternative to ...Kb2.
Kf2 approaches the trapped Ng1. The king on f2 covers e2, f3 and h3, so the black knight has no safe escape; White keeps a checked win.
branches.explanation: Kf2 approaches the trapped Ng1. The king on f2 covers e2, f3 and h3, so the black knight has no safe escape; White keeps a checked win.

exercises.answer: The knight on f4 controls both g2 and d3. Capturing g2 gives the black king d3, where it can stop the last white pawn.

exercises.prompt: Why move the king rather than push d4?
exercises.answer: Ke3 completes the cage around Ng1 without spending the pawn’s spare move. Advancing d4 first allows Black to draw with best play.

startContext: The complete five-piece setup is reconstructed from the saved boards. Selected source branches compare the drawing Nd6 route, Nd8+/Ke5/Ne6+/Nf4 coordination, the premature capture on g2, and the final reserve-tempo choice against ...g1=N. These selected lines are exact outcome checks, not a tree of every legal defense. The saved images supply the Nf4 move omitted in the rolling narration.
